title: Reconnaissance & Information Gathering
description: Techniques for mapping external attack surfaces, enumerating network and application assets, and harvesting sensitive intelligence prior to exploitation.

attacks.name: Subdomain enumeration
attacks.desc: Discovering unlinked, development, staging, or legacy subdomains belonging to a target domain using passive sources (Certificate Transparency, DNS aggregators) and active brute-forcing to uncover neglected assets.
attacks.prevention: Keep a complete subdomain inventory, retire unused hosts, and apply the same security controls to every environment; public DNS names cannot be hidden reliably.

attacks.name: DNS zone transfer (AXFR)
attacks.desc: Querying misconfigured authoritative DNS nameservers using AXFR requests to replicate the entire zone file, leaking comprehensive internal hostnames, IP allocations, and infrastructure topography.
attacks.prevention: Allow AXFR only to explicitly authorized secondary name servers, preferably over authenticated channels, and audit zone-transfer settings.

attacks.name: Virtual host discovery
attacks.desc: Fuzzing the HTTP 'Host' header on a single web server IP to discover distinct multi-tenant or private web applications hosted behind the same web server that lack public DNS records.
attacks.prevention: Reject unknown Host values at the edge and backend, and require explicit host allowlists for each virtual application.

attacks.name: Port & service scanning
attacks.desc: Probing target host network interfaces across TCP and UDP ports using syn, connect, or fragmented scans to identify reachable listening services and potential entry points.
attacks.prevention: Expose only required ports through firewalls or private networks, and keep reachable services patched and inventoried.

attacks.name: Service version fingerprinting
attacks.desc: Capturing service connection banners and inspecting protocol-specific response characteristics to determine exact daemon software names, patch levels, and associated public CVE vulnerabilities.
attacks.prevention: Limit unnecessary version banners, but prioritize timely patching because software can still be fingerprinted indirectly.

attacks.name: Technology stack fingerprinting
attacks.desc: Analyzing response headers, cookies, HTML source artifacts, scripts, and file structures to identify underlying frameworks, runtimes, database drivers, and programming languages.
attacks.prevention: Avoid exposing debug fingerprints and exact versions where possible; maintain and patch the actual stack instead of relying on obscurity.

attacks.name: CMS detection & version
attacks.desc: Identifying Content Management Systems and active plugins or themes through known paths (e.g. /wp-content/), meta generator tags, readme files, and static resource hashes.
attacks.prevention: Keep CMS core, themes, and plugins updated; remove unused components and restrict administrative access.

attacks.name: Directory & file brute forcing
attacks.desc: Executing high-velocity dictionary-based HTTP requests against a web root to discover unlinked directories, administrative panels, test interfaces, and unreferenced endpoints.
attacks.prevention: Treat every sensitive route as discoverable: enforce authentication and authorization on the server, regardless of its path.

attacks.name: Backup file discovery
attacks.desc: Searching for temporary, backup, or compressed files left behind by text editors and backup scripts (e.g. config.php.bak, db.sql, backup.zip) that expose sensitive raw source code or database dumps.
attacks.prevention: Store backups outside the public web root, deny direct access to backup extensions, and scan deployments for stray archives.

attacks.name: Exposed .git / .svn / .hg
attacks.desc: Downloading publicly accessible version control repository directories (such as /.git/) to reconstruct the entire application source tree, commit logs, internal author notes, and hardcoded secrets.

attacks.name: Exposed .env, config, credentials
attacks.desc: Accessing world-readable environment configuration files (e.g. /.env, /config.json, /web.config) containing production database credentials, encryption salts, third-party API tokens, and secret keys.

attacks.name: robots.txt / sitemap mining
attacks.desc: Inspecting crawler directive files like /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml to pinpoint high-value restricted directories, legacy modules, and internal portals explicitly disallowed from search indexing.

attacks.name: security.txt discovery
attacks.desc: Querying the RFC 9116 /.well-known/security.txt file to gather vulnerability disclosure policies, security contact channels, cryptographic signing keys, and organization scoping details.

attacks.name: Google / GitHub dorking
attacks.desc: Utilizing specialized search query syntax across public search engines and code repositories to discover indexed credentials, private staging subdomains, proprietary source code leaks, and open sensitive documents.

attacks.name: Certificate transparency mining
attacks.desc: Querying publicly verifiable append-only Certificate Transparency (CT) logs to identify newly minted or ephemeral SSL/TLS certificates issued for internal hostnames and subdomains.

attacks.name: Wayback Machine URL mining
attacks.desc: Scraping historical web snapshots from archival services to unearth deprecated REST API endpoints, forgotten parameters, outdated documentation, and previously exposed sensitive files.

attacks.name: JavaScript file mining
attacks.desc: Extracting, formatting, and analyzing client-side JavaScript bundles to identify hidden API routes, third-party credentials, internal hostnames, and developer comments disclosing system architecture.

attacks.name: Source map (.map) recovery
attacks.desc: Retrieving production .js.map and .ts.map files inadvertently deployed to production, allowing complete de-minification and recovery of pristine front-end TypeScript/JavaScript source code.

attacks.name: Parameter discovery
attacks.desc: Fuzzing HTTP query parameters, POST body parameters, and JSON payloads with specialized dictionaries to identify hidden or undocumented inputs that trigger debug or privileged functionality.

attacks.name: Metadata extraction
attacks.desc: Extracting hidden metadata from public documents, images, and media files to harvest employee usernames, internal software versions, corporate printer paths, and operating system builds.

attacks.name: Email / employee enumeration
attacks.desc: Gathering company email formatting standards, staff rosters, department directories, and engineering roles via OSINT platforms to prepare targeted spear-phishing and credential stuffing lists.

attacks.name: Cloud bucket enumeration
attacks.desc: Brute-forcing permutations of company names against cloud storage provider namespaces (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage) to locate misconfigured public data stores.

attacks.name: Secret scanning in repos
attacks.desc: Automating regex and entropy scanning over public or organization git commits to detect accidentally committed OAuth tokens, SSH private keys, AWS access keys, and cloud database strings.

attacks.name: ASN / IP range enumeration
attacks.desc: Mapping autonomous system numbers (ASNs) and IP CIDR blocks registered to an enterprise via BGP routing tables and WHOIS data to define the full perimeter of hosting infrastructure.

attacks.name: Subdomain takeover
attacks.desc: Claiming unallocated third-party cloud services (GitHub Pages, Heroku, AWS S3) pointed to by active DNS CNAME records, gaining full control over content served on the victim's domain.

attacks.name: Dangling DNS records
attacks.desc: Identifying obsolete A, AAAA, MX, or NS records pointing to decommissioned IP addresses or expired third-party domains, opening opportunities for traffic interception and impersonation.
